kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Most Complete Starter Kit

identity.canonical_name: DS3231 real-time clock (RTC) module, the widely sold "ZS-042" board with an onboard AT24C32N EEPROM chip and a CR2032 coin-cell battery holder
aliases: DS1307 RTC module (this is the name used in ELEGOO's own printed kit tutorial prose and its required code library for this exact lesson; both ELEGOO's own current online wiki page for the same lesson and an independently revised copy of this kit's tutorial on GitHub instead name the identical board a DS3231 module. See confidence.notes for the full second-pass resolution.)
identity.manufacturer: Timekeeping chip: most likely Analog Devices (formerly Maxim Integrated / Dallas Semiconductor) DS3231, per two independent second-pass sources (see confidence.notes). ELEGOO's own printed PDF tutorial text and required library name still say DS1307 (same manufacturer lineage either way). Breakout board manufacturer is generic/unconfirmed; the "ZS-042" board design is sold by many unbranded Chinese board houses.
identity.manufacturer_part_number: Most likely DS3231, not DS1307. Second-pass finding: an independently revised copy of this exact kit's tutorial, hosted on GitHub (rmorenojr/ElegooTutorial, Lesson 19), names this same lesson's part "ZS-042 Module aka. DS3231 RTC Module with AT24C32N EEprom chip and CR2032 battery," and its file listing includes a "DS3231 schematic.png" and an "AT24C32N datasheet.pdf" with no DS1307 files at all. A web search snippet of ELEGOO's own current wiki page for this same lesson (wiki.elegoo.com) contains the same wording almost verbatim, though that live page could not be made to load through a direct fetch this session (see confidence.notes), so it is not listed as a formal source. This matches the original finding that ELEGOO's own official kit PDF wiring diagram describes a 6-pin header with 32K and SQW pins, which the genuine DS1307 chip does not have per its datasheet (only the DS3231 family does). Countervailing evidence: ELEGOO also sells a genuinely-named spare part, "DS1307 Module V03," with a CR1220 battery, so a real DS1307-chip board is not impossible for some production runs or older kit revisions. Weighing it all, DS3231 is now the better-supported answer, but this is not fully closed for every physical unit; read the printed part number on the chip to confirm.
generic_equivalents: Any 6-pin I2C RTC breakout sharing this pinout, commonly sold as a "Tiny RTC" or "ZS-042" board, populated with either a DS3231 or (less commonly, per this second pass) a DS1307 chip on an otherwise near-identical PCB depending on the production run
identity.package: module (small breakout PCB with a coin-cell battery holder, a crystal or oscillator package, and a 6-pin header)

function.one_sentence_plain_english: This module keeps track of the date and time, even when the Arduino is turned off, thanks to a small backup battery.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used any time a project needs to know or display the current date and time, such as a clock, a data logger that timestamps readings, or an alarm.
function.how_it_works_briefly: A dedicated timekeeping chip counts seconds, minutes, hours, days, months, and years using its own crystal oscillator, and reports them to the Arduino over I2C. A small coin-cell battery keeps it running even when the Arduino's main power is unplugged.

pinout.name: 32K
pinout.notes: 32.768 kHz square wave output pin, left unused in ELEGOO's tutorial wiring. Confirmed as a standard DS3231-module pin by a generic DS3231 module reference page (lastminuteengineers.com). The genuine DS1307 chip has no equivalent separate pin per its datasheet, which is the main reason this second pass now favors DS3231 as the populated chip.

pinout.name: SQW
pinout.notes: On a DS3231 module this is usually silkscreened INT/SQW and is a configurable interrupt or square-wave output (per lastminuteengineers.com); on a genuine DS1307 chip the equivalent pin is a simpler open-drain SQW/OUT that needs an external pull-up (per the DS1307 datasheet). Left unused in ELEGOO's basic tutorial wiring either way.

pinout.name: SCL
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's SCL pin (analog pin 5), per ELEGOO's own tutorial.

pinout.name: SDA
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's SDA pin (analog pin 4), per ELEGOO's own tutorial. Open-drain and needs an external pull-up resistor; most breakout boards include this pull-up onboard.

pinout.name: VCC
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's 5V pin, per ELEGOO's own tutorial. See electrical.operating_voltage: the safe input range depends on which chip is actually populated, so treat this as 5V-only unless the chip marking confirms DS3231.

pinout.name: GND
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's GND pin.

pins.pin_1_identification: No numbered pin 1. The six pins are printed left to right on the header as 32K, SQW, SCL, SDA, VCC, GND, per ELEGOO's own tutorial wiring diagram. The coin-cell battery holder is the other clear identifying feature, and its size is itself a strong clue: a large, round CR2032 holder (20 mm across) points to a DS3231/ZS-042 board; a smaller CR1220 holder (12.5 mm across) points to ELEGOO's separately-listed "DS1307 Module V03" spare part.

electrical.operating_voltage: Depends on the actual populated chip, which this second pass narrowed but did not fully close. If the module is a DS3231 (now the better-supported identification): 2.3V to 5.5V, so it works safely down to 3.3V logic (per lastminuteengineers.com's DS3231 module reference). If the module is a genuine DS1307: 4.5V to 5.5V only, not safe to rely on at 3.3V (per the DS1307 datasheet). Because the chip cannot be told apart from a photo alone, treat any unconfirmed unit as 5V-only until the printed chip marking is read; running an unconfirmed board at 3.3V will not damage a DS3231 but may simply fail to work on a genuine DS1307, which is a safe way to narrow it down further (see troubleshooting).
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: -0.5V to +7.0V on any pin relative to ground (DS1307 datasheet, Dallas Semiconductor/Analog Devices). This figure is for the bare DS1307 chip; a DS3231-based board's absolute maximum was not separately confirmed this pass, so do not exceed 5.5V on VCC regardless of which chip is installed.
electrical.typical_current: up to 1.5 mA active supply current at 100 kHz SCL clocking (DS1307 datasheet); 300 nA typical battery-backup current at 25 degrees C with the oscillator running and SQW/OUT off (DS1307 datasheet). These figures are for the bare DS1307 chip only; DS3231-specific current figures were not confirmed by a fetched source this pass, so if the module turns out to be a DS3231 these numbers may not apply.
electrical.max_current: 1.5 mA active supply current maximum, 200 microamp standby current maximum, 500 nA battery-backup current maximum at 25 degrees C (DS1307 datasheet). Same caveat as typical_current: confirmed for the DS1307 chip only.
electrical.logic_level: 5V nominal on the header either way; SDA and SQW/INT are open-drain and need an external pull-up, normally already present on the breakout board. A DS3231-based board can additionally run its logic down to 3.3V (see operating_voltage); a genuine DS1307-based board cannot.

key_specs.timekeeping_fields: seconds, minutes, hours, day of week, date, month, year, with automatic leap-year correction valid through the year 2100 (DS1307 datasheet; the DS3231 provides the same set of fields over the same I2C interface).
key_specs.backup_ram: 56 bytes of battery-backed nonvolatile RAM built into the DS1307 chip (DS1307 datasheet). Not confirmed for a DS3231-based board, which instead commonly carries a separate AT24C32N EEPROM chip on the same PCB for user data storage (see below); the DS3231 chip itself has no equivalent onboard RAM.
key_specs.oscillator: external 32.768 kHz quartz crystal, 12.5 pF load capacitance (DS1307 datasheet, applies to the bare DS1307 chip).
key_specs.i2c_speed: up to 100 kHz, standard-mode I2C (DS1307 datasheet).
key_specs.backup_battery: Most likely a CR2032 lithium coin cell (the larger, 20 mm size). Second-pass source: an independently revised copy of this exact kit's tutorial on GitHub describes this same lesson's board as a "ZS-042 Module aka. DS3231 RTC Module with AT24C32N EEprom chip and CR2032 battery," and a search-engine snippet of ELEGOO's own current wiki page for the same lesson uses nearly identical wording. A separate, genuinely ELEGOO-branded spare-part listing for a "DS1307 Module V03" specifies the smaller CR1220 cell instead, so a CR1220 holder on a physical unit points to that different part.
key_specs.onboard_eeprom: Likely an AT24C32N I2C EEPROM chip (32 kilobit / 4 kilobyte) sharing the module's I2C bus, commonly found on DS3231/ZS-042 boards (per an independently revised copy of this kit's tutorial on GitHub, which lists an "AT24C32N datasheet.pdf" file alongside this lesson's materials). Not confirmed for a genuine DS1307-based ELEGOO module.

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Small rectangular PCB, roughly 2.7 cm x 2.8 cm, with a round coin-cell battery holder on one side and a 6-pin header along one edge.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: PCB color not independently confirmed for the ELEGOO-bundled unit (generic clone boards of this design are commonly sold in red, blue, or purple); a shiny round coin-cell battery sits in a metal spring clip; a small chip and an oscillator component sit near the header.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Header pins printed 32K SQW SCL SDA VCC GND, left to right. The single most reliable check: read the tiny printed part number on the black chip itself; it will read either "DS3231" or "DS1307" depending on which chip is actually installed, and that marking settles the question for that specific unit regardless of anything printed elsewhere on the board.
easily_confused_with: DS3231 / ZS-042 modules (identical or near-identical board shape and pin header layout; the coin-cell size, CR2032 versus the smaller CR1220, is a quick visual clue, and the printed chip marking is the definitive one)

required_extra_parts: 4 female-to-male Dupont wires (per ELEGOO's own kit tutorial)
a coin-cell battery to keep time when unplugged, if one is not already installed (CR2032 if the board is a DS3231/ZS-042, CR1220 if it is ELEGOO's separately listed DS1307 Module V03)
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: ELEGOO's own tutorial names a "DS1307" library, but this second pass found stronger evidence the populated chip is actually a DS3231 (see identity.manufacturer_part_number). A DS1307-only library will often fail to read a DS3231 chip correctly or at all. The Adafruit RTClib library supports both the DS1307 and the DS3231 and is the safer choice when the exact chip is not yet confirmed.

hazards: Reversed battery polarity can damage the coin-cell holder or the chip
Exceeding 5.5V on VCC risks damage on either chip
handling_notes: Handle the board by its edges
Avoid touching the battery contacts with wet hands
common_mistakes: Assuming any 6-pin RTC board is 3.3V-safe: only true if it is confirmed DS3231; a genuine DS1307-based board needs a full 5V supply to read and write over I2C reliably
Forgetting the backup battery, which causes the clock to reset to a default time whenever main power is removed

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Clock keeps resetting to a default date/time
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure the coin-cell voltage directly with a multimeter; a healthy 3V lithium cell should read close to 3V

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: No I2C response from the module
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: SDA and SCL swapped, or the module isn't getting 5V
symptoms_and_causes.check: Run an I2C scanner sketch and confirm the RTC answers at its address; verify 5V is reaching the VCC pin

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Uncertain whether the installed chip is DS1307 or DS3231
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Board silkscreen and printed tutorial name disagree (see confidence.notes)
symptoms_and_causes.check: First, read the tiny printed part number on the black chip directly; this is definitive. If the marking cannot be read, note the coin-cell size (CR2032 leans DS3231, CR1220 leans DS1307), then power the module from 3.3V logic instead of 5V and run an I2C scanner: a DS3231 will typically still respond at 3.3V, while a genuine DS1307 usually will not respond reliably below its 4.5V minimum. This 3.3V test will not damage either chip, since both tolerate down to well below 3.3V without exceeding any rated maximum.

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the Arduino powered, measure between the module's VCC and GND pins; expect a reading close to 5V. To check the backup battery alone, measure directly across its contacts; expect a reading close to 3V.

confidence.notes: Second research pass, resolving the open question from the first pass (DS1307 named in ELEGOO's tutorial text vs. a DS3231-style 32K/SQW pinout in that same tutorial's wiring diagram). New evidence found: (1) an independently revised copy of this exact kit's tutorial, hosted on GitHub at rmorenojr/ElegooTutorial, Lesson 19, names this same lesson's part "ZS-042 Module aka. DS3231 RTC Module with AT24C32N EEprom chip and CR2032 battery," and its file listing includes "DS3231 schematic.png" and "AT24C32N datasheet.pdf" with no DS1307 files anywhere; (2) a web search of ELEGOO's own current wiki page for this same lesson (wiki.elegoo.com/oshw-getting-started-kits/RealTimeClock-uno) returned an indexed snippet with nearly identical wording ("the kit includes a DS3231 RTC Module with AT24C32N EEprom chip and CR2032 battery"), but this page could not be made to fully load through a direct fetch this session (it returned only a title and breadcrumb once, and a 404 on retry, likely because the page renders its content via JavaScript), so it is not listed as a formal source, only reported here as corroborating context; (3) re-reading ELEGOO's own official kit PDF (via pdftotext this pass) confirmed the exact prose again: the lesson's Overview and Component Introduction both say "DS1307," the wiring instructions say to "ignore the 32K and SQW pins," and a NOTICE states that an "old version" and a "new version" of the board share the same pin functions and names, meaning ELEGOO's own material acknowledges more than one hardware revision has shipped under this same lesson. Weighed together, this second pass now favors DS3231 as the more likely populated chip and sets identity.canonical_name accordingly, with DS1307 demoted to an alias, but does not call this fully closed: a genuinely ELEGOO-branded "DS1307 Module V03" spare part (CR1220 battery) still exists and could be what ships in some runs. The rule for a technician holding a physical unit: read the tiny printed part number on the black chip itself first (definitive); if unreadable, the coin-cell size is a fast visual proxy (CR2032, 20 mm, leans DS3231; CR1220, 12.5 mm, leans DS1307); as a last resort, the 3.3V-power-and-I2C-scan test in troubleshooting can distinguish the two without risking damage to either chip.
